scenes.title: 1964 Oxford Dichotic Console: Mid-Sentence Story Swap Pulling the Listener's Voice Across Headphone Ears + Dimmer-Knob Threshold Board
scenes.era: 1964, Institute of Experimental Psychology, University of Oxford

layout.description: Sunlit high-key 1964 Oxford psychology laboratory featuring a clean brushed-aluminum **dual-channel studio audio console** wired to **padded over-ear headphones**, a glowing **Attenuator Rotary Dimmer Dial** contrast plaque ('Broadbent ON/OFF Switch [Wrong] vs Treisman Dimmer Knob: 86.5% Attended / 8.7% Attenuated'), and a split sentence-swap card showing **Right Ear: 'SITTING AT A MAHOGANY -> [random words]'** crossing diagonally into **Left Ear: '-> TABLE WITH HER HEAD!'**.

positions.who: Anne Treisman (mannequin in 1964 tailored Oxford cardigan twinset and skirt)
positions.where: seated at the dual-channel studio audio console flipping the silent mid-sentence crossover switch while tracking the listener's spoken words on her transcript sheet

positions.who: Oxford Student Listener mannequin (wearing padded over-ear headphones in 1964 V-neck sweater)
positions.where: shadowing the Right Ear briskly aloud — accidentally blurting out **'TABLE!'** from the ignored Left Ear right at the crossover, then blinking in amused surprise!

props.name: dual-channel studio audio console & padded headphones
Diagonal Sentence-Crossover Card ('Right Ear: MAHOGANY \ Left Ear: TABLE!')
Dictionary Threshold Bar Chart ('Random Word: High Bar | Primed Word & [OWN NAME]: Hair-Trigger Low Bar!')
props.period_detail: shows how a small 10% attenuated signal clears a low bar while missing a high bar
props.physical_behavior: explains the Cocktail Party own-name effect

actions.verb_sequence: flips the silent channel-crossover switch mid-sentence -> Listener's mouth automatically follows the meaningful sentence onto the 'ignored' Left Ear for two words before snapping back to the Right Ear
points on the Threshold Bar Chart showing why attenuated signals clear low-threshold '[Own Name]' and primed words (86.5% vs 8.7%)

reactions.reaction: laughs realizing their own mouth proved the 'ignored' ear wasn't 100% off!
smiles reconciling Early vs Late Selection in one stroke

scenes.wardrobe: 1964 British Oxford academic style: classic knit cardigan twinset and pleated skirt; collegiate V-neck jumper over Oxford shirt.
scenes.lighting: Warm, bright high-key Oxford window daylight.
scenes.recognition_hook: Swap the story into the 'ignored' headphone cup mid-sentence, and the listener's own mouth blurts out the jumped word before they even realize it!

key_visual.description: a 1964 Oxford lab with a researcher at a dual-channel studio audio console and a diagonal sentence-crossover chart as a listener in padded headphones blurts out the jumped word

scenes.title: 1964 Bilingual Proof: Hearing the Same Meaning Across English & French!

layout.description: Bright testing booth where an English-French bilingual shadows English in the Right Ear while French plays softly offset in the Left Ear.

positions.where: raising a hand smiling: 'Wait — the French speaker in my left ear is translating the exact same story!'

props.name: English Right / French Left parallel script card
props.period_detail: proves attenuated input reaches deep conceptual meaning, not just English word sounds

actions.verb_sequence: offsets French translation slightly in Left Ear -> Bilingual spots the shared story meaning

scenes.recognition_hook: Strangers miss foreign German completely — yet play a French translation of the SAME story to a bilingual, and primed concepts recognize their twin!

scenes.title: 1967 Ruler-Tap Showdown: 86.5% vs 8.7% Settles the Filter War

layout.description: Clean table where a shadowing listener holds a wooden ruler to tap the desk whenever a target word occurs in EITHER ear.

positions.where: tapping crisply 86.5% of the time for Right-Ear targets vs only 8.7% for Left-Ear targets

props.name: 86.5% Attended vs 8.7% Unattended bar plaque & wooden tap ruler

actions.verb_sequence: taps reliably on attended targets while missing 9 out of 10 ordinary unattended targets

scenes.recognition_hook: Not zero percent and not a hundred percent — 86.5% vs 8.7% proved human attention is a biological dimmer switch!

scenes.title: The 'Name-First' Rule in Cockpits, Operating Rooms & Home
scenes.era: Modern hospital surgical / aviation communication room

layout.description: Sunlit modern clinical station where a nurse says 'Dr. Patel — [half-second pause as head turns] — potassium is 3.1' instead of blurting numbers first.

positions.where: speaking the doctor's name first to trip the low-threshold alarm
turning full 100% attention immediately BEFORE the critical number is spoken

props.name: Name -> Pause -> Data communication card
props.period_detail: harnesses Treisman's low-threshold own-name trigger to prevent missed medical/cockpit numbers

actions.verb_sequence: says Name first -> waits 0.5s for eye contact -> delivers number at 100% gain

reactions.reaction: zero missed numbers under busy workload

scenes.recognition_hook: Never start an urgent sentence with the number — start with their NAME so Treisman's hair-trigger switch turns their dimmer knob up to 100%!
